quotes: Comparing k-mer content across genomes needs a hash that gives a k-mer and its reverse complement one value. For k-mers that fit a machine word, a canonical packed code and a universal hash give one with a proof, but longer k-mers and spaced seeds lack that route, and the rolling hashes ntHash and ntHash2 carry no proven collision bound. We read a k-mer as a polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_q$, $q = 2^{61} - 1$, with bases at sixth roots of unity, a published encoding in which complement is negation. The product $(F + \lambda)(R + \lambda)$ of the two strand evaluations is then the same for both strands, and distinct double-stranded k-mers collide with probability at most $2(k-1)/q$, $2.6 \times 10^{-17}$ at $k = 31$, for every input. Power sums of these hashes form a linear set sketch that needs no canonicalization. Between two cannabis assemblies differing in 3.2 million 31-mers, it recovered every difference in 30 of 30 runs, each party sending 11.3 bytes per difference over two rounds. Hashing every k-mer takes 2.2 times as long as a batched ntHash, and a sampler that hashes 1 in 1,000 k-mers runs 1.21 times as fast, about as fast as the same sampler with a universal hash.

Field values also add. Power sums of the hashes form a linear sketch from which a set difference can be recovered exactly [@dodis_2008_fuzzy-extractors; @minsky_2003_set-reconciliation; @naumenko_2019_erlay]. The sketch spreads the difference over buckets and checks each one, so a bucket that holds too many differences is split and resent on its own in a second round. The invertible Bloom lookup table we compare against is resent whole, although a table can instead grow by sending only its new cells [@mitzenmacher_2017_multiparty-reconciliation] or be made rateless [@yang_2024_rateless-reconciliation]. When the hash is strand-symmetric, so is the sketch, without canonicalizing anything first. Between a cannabis assembly and its draft, the sketch of k-mers as written recovered the 7,931 differing k-mers exactly, where a forward-only polynomial hash faced 398 million.

A sketch of a k-mer set assigns each strand-symmetric hash $h$ to one of $2^b$ buckets and stores, per bucket, the count and the power sums $\sum h^j$ for $j = 1, \ldots, m + c$ [@dodis_2008_fuzzy-extractors; @naumenko_2019_erlay]. The sketch is linear. The sketch of a union of disjoint sets is the sum of their sketches, and subtracting the sketches of two sets leaves the signed power sums of their symmetric difference. Newton's identities and a Padé step recover up to $m$ differences per bucket and say which set each came from [@minsky_2003_set-reconciliation]. The $c$ extra sums check the result, so a bucket holding more than $m$ differences is detected, except with small probability over the random hash. It is then split and resent, at the cost of one more round [@minsky_2002_practical-reconciliation; @naumenko_2019_erlay]. Each entry is one field element of 8 bytes, in either field. The whole-genome comparison used a C implementation over the Eisenstein field with $m = 64$ and $c = 2$. It hashes every 31-mer as written, with no canonical code, so only $S$ supplies strand symmetry, and a bucket is a range of $S$. Both parties send a sketch, a bucket is accepted when both sides' checks pass, and each party finds its own differing k-mers by rescanning its genome for the recovered values. The first round uses the smallest power of two of buckets that holds at most $0.8m$ estimated differences each. We chose $m$ and $2^{16}$ buckets for size on 1/64 of the GigaDB pair and set the $0.8m$ rule to reproduce them, as km-peeler's table size was chosen on 4 of its 64 parts. We ran it from the true difference and from estimates between one eighth and four times it. The $k = 63$ run hashed with the same C code and reconciled in a numpy prototype, with $2^{10}$ buckets sized from the true difference, an average of 20.9 differences each.

The reference roller follows the two update rules above. The fast rollers keep $G = F + \lambda$ and $H = R + \lambda$ as the rolling state, so the constant $\lambda$ never needs adding per k-mer. They merge the two per-strand table lookups into one 16-entry table indexed by the outgoing and incoming base, and leave additions partly reduced until the next multiplication. A batch loop hashes a run of k-mers with the state in registers, and an interleaved version rolls two contiguous stretches of a block together so their dependency chains overlap. The Eisenstein roller needs three modular multiplications per k-mer, one per strand and one for $S$. Seeds for $x$ and $\lambda$ are drawn independently, from the operating system by default. Most experiments used fixed seeds for reproducibility, so they test the construction rather than the bound. The 30 runs per pair of the sketch comparison drew their seeds from the operating system.

We compared the power-sum sketch with km-peeler, the invertible Bloom lookup tables of Shibuya, Belazzougui and Kucherov [@shibuya_2022_genomic-reconciliation; @goodrich_2011_iblt; @eppstein_2011_set-difference], on two pairs of cannabis assemblies. Cannbio-2 and its GigaDB release differ in 3,238,101 canonical 31-mers, 0.73 percent of the set, all but 775 of them in Cannbio-2. Cannbio-2 and its draft differ in 7,931. KMC [@kokot_2017_counting] confirmed both differences element by element. km-peeler ran unmodified with its default three hash functions on the canonical k-mer sets of both assemblies. Each method ran 30 times on one host, the sketch with seeds from the operating system and km-peeler with seeds 1001 to 1030, from which it derives its hash functions as seed, seed + 1 and seed + 2, so neighbouring trials share two.
| power-sum sketch, one party's message | 11.3 | in 30 of 30 runs | 2 |
| power-sum sketch with twice the buckets | 21.7 | yes, in one run | 1 |
| km-peeler, k-mer table, 1.28 cells per difference | 20.5 | in 30 of 30 trials | 1 |
| km-peeler, extended syncmers, earlier run | 4.2 | no, 1,986,807 spurious k-mers and 7 missed | 1 |

: Recovering the GigaDB difference, $k = 31$. Bytes are as each implementation stores them: 8-byte field elements for the sketch, and 16-byte cells for km-peeler, half of each a 64-bit counter. The sketch started from $2^{16}$ buckets and split about 1,250 of them, sending about 2,500 halves in its second round. The k-mer table was sized to succeed in 30 of 30 trials. The extended-syncmer row is an earlier run of five trials.

Between the two assemblies, each party sent a sketch of 11.3 bytes per difference over two rounds, 22.5 in all, and the two parties recovered every difference exactly in 30 of 30 runs, each its own. One message of km-peeler's table, 20.5 bytes per difference, gave both sides in one round. The sketch's cost also depends on where the difference falls between powers of two of buckets. This pair sits 3.5 percent below a doubling, and with twice the buckets the sketch finished in one round at 21.7. The sketch's 30 of 30 bounds its failure rate below 9.5 percent (one-sided, 95 percent), while the table's trials share hash functions and are not independent. Neither method returned a wrong difference. The sketch can still miss one: an overfull bucket escapes its check with small probability, and a differing k-mer that collides with one the other party holds cancels unseen, which the bound puts below 0.04 times per run here. When the difference was underestimated eightfold, the sketch ended exact at 20.8 bytes per difference per party, while km-peeler's table, resent at double size, ended at 38.5 (Figure 4B). Each grew by about the same factor, 1.84 and 1.87 times its cost at the true difference, and a table that sends only its new cells would total about 20.5, by arithmetic [@mitzenmacher_2017_multiparty-reconciliation]. These underestimates are imposed: here the two set sizes alone give the difference within 0.05 percent. The 7,931 differences between an assembly and its draft all lie on the draft's side, so one sketch of 17.3 bytes per difference sufficed, against 20.5 for the table, half of whose bytes are 64-bit counters that a packed table would shrink. These results come from one genome and two pairs.

![The sketch resends only overfull buckets. (A) Each bucket, a range of $S$, holds the count and the power sums $\sum h^j$, $j = 1, \ldots, m + c$. Subtracting two sketches leaves the signed power sums of the difference. A bucket with more than $m$ differences fails its check, except with small probability, and is split and resent alone in the next round. (B) Bytes per difference in one party's messages between Cannbio-2 and its GigaDB release, with buckets or table sized from an estimate that is the difference divided by a power of two. The km-peeler table is resent at double size after each failed listing, so its last listing always lands on its tuned size, its cheapest case. Labels give the rounds. Both methods ended exact at every point, the sketch in one fixed-seed run per point and the table identically in all 10 repetitions.](figures/fig4_sketch.pdf)

The sketch hashed k-mers as written. The draft writes 45 percent of its bases on contigs in the other orientation, so a forward-only polynomial hash, in the numpy prototype of the same sketch ($2^8$ buckets, $m = 64$, $c = 2$), faced 398,217,248 differences and overflowed every bucket. At $k = 63$, the hash, computed from the sequence with no packed code, recovered all 21,382 differences in 549 KB and one round, at an average of 20.9 differences per bucket. The result matched the canonical difference computed by KMC element by element. The extended-syncmer method of km-peeler, which its authors propose for recovering every difference, also reads each assembly as written. In an earlier run of five trials on the GigaDB pair it was 2.7 times smaller than our sketch but returned spurious k-mers numbering 61 percent of the true difference, against about 3 percent in the authors' tests on viral and simulated genomes, and missed the same 7 differences in every trial. We did not trace either. Between draft and final, 48,293,748 extended syncmers differed, and the run ran out of memory while listing.

Building the sketch costs $m + c = 66$ field multiplications per element, against 3 cell updates for the table, and recovery adds about 50 more per element on the GigaDB pair. On one thread, the sketch took 89 CPU seconds to build per side and 110 to recover the difference, against 205 and 3.5 for km-peeler, whose build parses k-mer text, and 326 against about 460 from genomes to recovered k-mers.

For k-mers that fit a machine word, a canonical packed code and a universal hash already give strand symmetry with a proven bound, and in our measurements they ran 1.12 times as fast as batched ntHash. Chained through each benchmark program's own ntHash, they ran 2.4 times as fast as our hash. The strand-symmetric product should earn its place where that recipe is costly or unavailable: for long k-mers, where canonical codes span several words, for spaced seeds and for values that must be added when $k > 32$. It gives a collision bound for every pair of inputs, strand symmetry by factorization and a field in which the hashes themselves form a linear set sketch. That sketch recovered every difference between two assemblies with 22.5 bytes per difference in all, against 20.5 for one message of km-peeler's table. Without canonicalization it recovered every difference between an assembly and its draft at $k = 31$ and $k = 63$, where a strand-specific hash faced 398 million at $k = 31$. A table of canonical k-mers is orientation-blind too, so this shows that the hash supplies the symmetry, not that it beats canonicalization.

outcome: The user's claims 4-6.
